title: Title IX and a New Door
bigQuestion: How did a short education law from 1972 change who plays school sports, and why did it take courts, rules and decades to do it?

story.title: One Board, Two Papers
story.kicker: A copy of a federal law hangs beside a brand-new team list.
paragraphs: It is the winter of 2022 in an Illinois high school. A cork bulletin board hangs outside the athletic office. Someone has pinned up a printed page with one long sentence on it. The sentence comes from a federal law passed fifty years earlier, in 1972.

Next to it hangs a roster, a list of team members. It is for girls wrestling. This season, 2021–22, is the first in which the Illinois High School Association runs girls wrestling as its own sport. The first girls state finals will be held this February.

Boys in Illinois have had IHSA state wrestling champions since 1937. That is eighty-five years earlier. For much of that time, a girl who wanted to wrestle had to join a boys team, if a school let her.

The law on the left never uses the word sport. It talks about education programs that get money from the federal government. Yet students, parents, lawyers and judges used that one sentence to open doors in gyms and on fields across the country.
story.think: How can a law that never mentions sports change who gets to play?

lessons.title: Play Days Instead of Titles
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1920s many women physical educators pushed girls toward play days instead of championships.
reading: In 1923 a group called the *Women's Division* of the National Amateur Athletic Federation formed. Lou Henry Hoover, wife of the future president Herbert Hoover, was one of its leaders. Its members were mostly women who taught physical education in schools and colleges.

The Women's Division opposed star players, big crowds and championships for girls. Its leaders worried that fierce contests would harm girls or turn them into entertainment for paying fans. They favored *play days*, where students from several schools were mixed onto new teams for friendly games.

The idea spread widely. By the 1930s many high schools and colleges had few interschool contests for girls. Some states, such as Iowa, kept strong girls basketball, but in much of the country girls' sport was kept small on purpose.

Historians read this in two ways. Women teachers did control girls' sport and shaped it by their own values. But the result was that girls had far fewer teams, coaches and trophies than boys for decades.

words.d: a group formed in 1923, led by women educators, that shaped girls' sport and opposed championships
an event where students from several schools were mixed onto teams for friendly games, not titles

look.title: A Play Day Program
look.text: Picture a printed program from about 1930. Girls from four schools meet at one gym. Each girl wears a colored ribbon. Teams are named Red, Blue, Green and Gold, not by school. No scores are posted and no trophy is given. Tea is served afterward.
look.prompt: What did the organizers want girls to get from this day? What did it leave out that boys' teams had?

check.q: What did the Women's Division favor for girls?
choices: Boys and girls on one team
check.why: The Women's Division favored play days over interschool championships.

check.q: Who was a leader of the Women's Division?
check.why: Lou Henry Hoover helped lead the Women's Division formed in 1923.

check.q: What was one result of the play day approach?
choices: Girls got more trophies than boys
Girls' sport moved to the Olympics
Girls had far fewer teams and coaches than boys
check.why: Keeping girls' sport small left them with fewer teams, coaches and trophies for decades.

lessons.title: Counting Players
lessons.mainIdea: In 1971–72 about 294,000 high school girls played school sports, compared with about 3.67 million boys.
reading: Since the early 1970s, the *National Federation of State High School Associations*, or NFHS, has counted players each year. It asks every state association, including the IHSA, how many students played school sports. These counts let historians compare one year with another.

In the 1971–72 school year, the NFHS counted 294,015 girls. It counted 3,666,917 boys. That means about one athlete in every thirteen was a girl. Many schools had no girls teams at all in some sports.

One year later, in 1972–73, the girls count had risen to 817,073. By 2018–19 it was 3,402,733. The count of boys also rose, but the gap narrowed. A *participation* count does not show quality of coaching or fields, but it shows who had a spot on a roster.

words.w: National Federation of State High School Associations
words.d: the national group of state school sports bodies, which counts high school players each year
taking part; in sports records, the number of students on school teams

look.title: High School Girls on School Teams
look.cite: National Federation of State High School Associations, High School Athletics Participation Survey
look.prompt: About how many times larger was the 2018–19 count than the 1971–72 count?

check.q: About how many girls played high school sports in 1971–72?
check.why: The NFHS counted 294,015 girls in 1971–72.

check.q: Who collects the national count of high school athletes?
check.why: The National Federation of State High School Associations gathers counts from each state association.

check.q: What does a participation count NOT show?
choices: The quality of coaching or fields
check.why: It counts roster spots, not quality of coaching or facilities.

lessons.title: The IHSA Adds Girls' Titles
lessons.mainIdea: The IHSA, founded in 1900 for boys' contests, began adding state series for girls in the 1970s.
reading: The Illinois High School Association was founded in 1900. It is a voluntary *association*: member schools agree to follow its rules and send teams to its state series. For most of the 1900s its state champions were boys' teams.

Boys basketball held its first IHSA state tournament in 1908. Boys wrestling crowned its first state champions in 1937. Girls in Illinois had school clubs and some meets, but no IHSA state title in most sports.

In the 1970s the IHSA began state series for girls. Girls basketball held its first IHSA state tournament in 1977. Each new *state series* meant new rules, officials, schedules and a trophy for girls across Illinois.

words.d: a group whose members agree to follow shared rules
the chain of regional and state contests that ends in a state championship

look.title: Reading a Trophy Case
look.text: A school trophy case in Illinois holds boys basketball trophies from the 1920s, 1950s and 1960s. The first girls trophy is dated 1978. All the trophies are shiny, but the dates tell a story.
look.prompt: What can the dates in the case tell a visitor about when the IHSA offered girls a state title?

check.q: When was the IHSA founded?
check.why: The IHSA was founded in 1900.

check.q: When did IHSA girls basketball hold its first state tournament?
check.why: IHSA girls basketball held its first state tournament in 1977.

check.q: What is a state series?
choices: The chain of contests ending in a state title
check.why: A state series is the run of contests that ends in a state championship.

lessons.title: Thirty-Seven Words
lessons.mainIdea: Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972 bans sex discrimination in federally funded education programs.
reading: On June 23, 1972, President Richard Nixon signed the *Education Amendments of 1972*. It was a long bill about schools and colleges. Its ninth part, or *Title IX*, was one sentence of thirty-seven words.

In the Senate, Birch Bayh of Indiana sponsored it. In the House, Edith Green of Oregon and Patsy Mink of Hawaii worked for it. Mink was the first woman of color elected to Congress. After her death, Congress renamed the law the Patsy T. Mink Equal Opportunity in Education Act in 2002.

The sentence covers any education program that receives *federal financial assistance*, meaning money from the national government. Nearly every public school and most colleges receive such money. So the law reached almost every school in the country.

The words sport and athletics do not appear in the sentence. Supporters mainly had admissions, hiring and classes in mind. But school teams are an education program, so the sentence applied to them too.

words.d: the part of the Education Amendments of 1972 that bans sex discrimination in federally funded education
the federal school law, signed June 23, 1972, that contains Title IX
money a school or program receives from the national government

look.title: The Sentence Itself
look.text: No person in the United States shall, on the basis of sex, be excluded from participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be subjected to discrimination under any education program or activity receiving Federal financial assistance.
look.cite: Title IX, Education Amendments of 1972, 20 U.S.C. § 1681(a)
look.prompt: Find the three things the law says no person may suffer. Which of them could apply to a school team?

check.q: Who signed the Education Amendments of 1972?
check.why: President Nixon signed the law on June 23, 1972.

check.q: Which senator sponsored Title IX?
check.why: Birch Bayh of Indiana sponsored Title IX in the Senate.

check.q: Why did Title IX reach almost every school?
choices: Nearly all schools receive federal money
It was added to every state constitution
check.why: The law covers programs receiving federal financial assistance, which includes nearly all schools.

lessons.title: Amendments and Rules, 1974–1975
lessons.mainIdea: Congress rejected a plan to exempt money-making sports in 1974, and federal rules in 1975 applied Title IX to athletics.
reading: A law often needs *regulations*: detailed rules written by a government agency to explain how it works. For Title IX, the agency was the Department of Health, Education, and Welfare, called HEW. While HEW wrote them, college sports leaders pushed back.

In 1974 Senator John Tower of Texas proposed exempting sports that earned money, such as college football, from Title IX. Congress rejected the *Tower Amendment*. Instead it passed the Javits Amendment, from Senator Jacob Javits of New York, asking HEW to write reasonable rules for sports.

HEW issued the regulations in 1975, and President Gerald Ford signed them. They said schools must offer equal opportunity in athletics. Schools could keep separate teams for girls and boys. Elementary schools had until 1976 to comply, and high schools and colleges until 1978.

words.d: detailed rules an agency writes to explain how a law is carried out
a 1974 proposal, rejected by Congress, to exempt money-making sports from Title IX
to follow a rule or law

look.title: Two Amendments Side by Side
look.text: Tower Amendment, 1974: leave out sports that earn money from Title IX. Javits Amendment, 1974: ask the agency to write reasonable rules for sports, taking into account the nature of each sport.
look.prompt: Congress passed one and rejected the other. What did that choice mean for college football?

check.q: What did the Tower Amendment propose?
choices: Exempting money-making sports from Title IX
Moving Title IX to the IOC
check.why: Tower wanted revenue sports like football left out; Congress rejected it.

check.q: Which agency wrote the first Title IX regulations?
choices: The Department of Health, Education, and Welfare
check.why: HEW wrote the regulations, issued in 1975.

check.q: By what year did high schools and colleges have to comply?
check.why: The 1975 regulations gave high schools and colleges until 1978.

lessons.title: The Three-Part Test, 1979
lessons.mainIdea: A 1979 federal policy gave schools three ways to show they offer girls and boys a fair chance to play.
reading: Schools asked how to prove they were following the law. In December 1979 HEW issued a *policy interpretation*. It explained how the agency would judge athletics. Its best-known part is called the *three-part test*.

A school passes if it meets any one of three parts. First, the share of athletes who are women is close to the share of students who are women. Second, the school has a history of adding teams for the sex with fewer chances. Third, the school fully meets the interests and abilities of that sex.

The first part is often called *proportionality*. It became the most argued-over part, because a school could meet it by adding women's teams or by cutting men's teams. Supporters and critics have debated it ever since, in courts and in Congress.

words.d: an agency's official explanation of how it will apply a law or regulation
the 1979 standard that lets a school show fair athletic opportunity in any one of three ways
matching the share of women athletes to the share of women students

look.title: A College to Judge
look.text: A college has 5,000 students, and half are women. It has 400 athletes, and 150 are women. It added a women's soccer team five years ago and nothing since. Some women students have asked for a softball team.
look.prompt: Using the three parts, does this college pass any part? Explain with the numbers.

check.q: How many parts of the test must a school meet?
check.why: A school passes by meeting any one of the three parts.

check.q: What does proportionality compare?
choices: The share of women athletes and women students
The number of coaches and fields
check.why: Proportionality matches women's share of athletes to their share of students.

check.q: Why is proportionality argued over?
choices: It was written by the IOC
Schools can meet it by cutting men's teams
check.why: A school can meet it by adding women's teams or by cutting men's teams, which is debated.

lessons.title: Grove City and the 1988 Law
lessons.mainIdea: A 1984 Supreme Court case narrowed Title IX, and Congress restored its reach in 1988 over a presidential veto.
reading: Grove City College is a small private college in Pennsylvania. It took no federal money directly, but some students paid tuition with federal grants. The college refused to sign a Title IX form, and the case reached the Supreme Court.

In *Grove City College v. Bell*, decided in February 1984, the Court said Title IX covered only the specific program that received federal money. At most colleges, the athletic department got no federal money directly. So for a time Title IX barely reached sports.

Congress answered with the *Civil Rights Restoration Act of 1988*. It said the law covers a whole school if any part receives federal money. President Ronald Reagan vetoed the bill. In March 1988 Congress overrode his veto, and the act became law.

words.d: a 1984 Supreme Court case that limited Title IX to the program receiving federal money
the law, passed over a veto, that made Title IX cover a whole school
a president's rejection of a bill, which Congress can override with a two-thirds vote in each house

look.title: One College, Two Readings
look.text: Reading A (1984): only the office that handles federal student grants must follow Title IX. Reading B (1988): if any part of the college gets federal money, the whole college must follow Title IX, including its teams.
look.prompt: Under each reading, must the college's basketball team follow Title IX? Explain.

check.q: What did the Court decide in Grove City College v. Bell?
choices: Title IX covered only the program getting federal money
check.why: The 1984 ruling limited Title IX to the specific program receiving federal money.

check.q: How did the Civil Rights Restoration Act become law?
choices: It passed with no votes against
check.why: Reagan vetoed the bill, and Congress overrode the veto in March 1988.

check.q: When did Congress restore Title IX's wide reach?
check.why: The Civil Rights Restoration Act of 1988 restored it.

lessons.title: The AIAW and the NCAA
lessons.mainIdea: Women ran their own college sports body, the AIAW, from 1971 until the NCAA took over women's championships in the early 1980s.
reading: In 1971 women athletic leaders founded the *Association for Intercollegiate Athletics for Women*, or AIAW. It ran national championships for college women in many sports. Women coaches and administrators led it, and it set its own rules on scholarships and recruiting.

The *NCAA*, the National Collegiate Athletic Association, governed men's college sport. At first it had fought parts of Title IX. After the law took hold, it decided to offer women's championships itself, starting in the 1981–82 school year.

Many colleges moved their women's teams to the NCAA, which had more money and television deals. The AIAW sued the NCAA, claiming it broke laws against unfair competition, and lost. The AIAW closed in 1982. Historians note that women gained NCAA titles but lost a body women had built and led.

words.d: the Association for Intercollegiate Athletics for Women, a body run by women that governed college women's sport from 1971 to 1982
the National Collegiate Athletic Association, the main governing body of college sport in the United States

look.title: Gain and Loss
look.text: In 1980 a women's college basketball coach answers to the AIAW, a body run mostly by women. In 1983 the same coach's team plays for an NCAA title, under an organization led mostly by men, with a bigger budget.
look.prompt: List one thing the coach gained and one thing she lost in the change.

check.q: When was the AIAW founded?
check.why: Women leaders founded the AIAW in 1971.

check.q: Which school year did the NCAA begin women's championships?
check.why: The NCAA started women's championships in 1981–82.

check.q: What happened to the AIAW in 1982?
choices: It closed after losing its suit against the NCAA
check.why: The AIAW lost its lawsuit and closed in 1982.

lessons.title: Cohen v. Brown University
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1990s women athletes at Brown University sued after teams were cut and won a major Title IX ruling.
reading: In 1991 Brown University in Rhode Island cut four teams to save money. Two were women's teams, gymnastics and volleyball. Two were men's teams. Amy Cohen, a gymnast, and other women athletes sued the university in a *class action*, a case brought for a whole group.

Brown argued that women were less interested in sports than men, so fewer spots for women were fair. The women argued that Brown failed all three parts of the 1979 test. The share of women among athletes was well below their share of students.

In 1996 the federal *appeals court* for the region ruled for the women athletes. It said interest cannot be judged by counting who already plays, because past chances shape interest. In 1997 the Supreme Court declined to hear Brown's appeal, so the ruling stood.

words.d: a lawsuit brought on behalf of a whole group of people
a higher court that reviews the decision of a lower court

look.title: The Court's Reasoning
look.text: The appeals court said that interest in sports grows from opportunity. Counting how many women already play cannot prove women are less interested, since the lack of teams is part of why fewer play.
look.cite: Cohen v. Brown University, U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit, 1996
look.prompt: Explain the court's point in your own words. Can you think of another place where chances shape interest?

check.q: Why did the Brown athletes sue?
choices: They wanted to play on men's teams
check.why: Brown cut women's gymnastics and volleyball in 1991, and the athletes sued.

check.q: What is a class action?
choices: A lawsuit for a whole group
check.why: A class action is brought on behalf of a group, as the Brown athletes did.

check.q: What happened when Brown appealed to the Supreme Court in 1997?
choices: The Court declined to hear it
The case was sent to the IOC
check.why: The Supreme Court declined review, so the 1996 ruling stood.

lessons.title: Wrestling Since 1937
lessons.mainIdea: IHSA boys wrestling has crowned state champions since 1937, while girls long had no state series of their own.
reading: The IHSA crowned its first boys wrestling state champions in 1937. From then on, Illinois boys had a full *weight class* system, sectional meets and a state final each winter. Schools hired coaches and bought mats for these teams.

For decades girls had no IHSA wrestling series. Some girls joined boys teams and wrestled boys in matches, where schools allowed it. National groups outside school sport, such as USA Wrestling, held girls' events. Women's wrestling joined the Olympic program at the 2004 Athens Games.

The gap shows how an *institution* can open a door slowly. Title IX required fair chances overall, but it did not require a girls team in every sport. A state association still had to vote to create a new state series.

words.d: a group of competitors of similar body weight who compete against each other
an organization with rules that lasts over time, such as a school association

look.title: First IHSA State Titles in Three Sports
look.unit: year of first IHSA state title
look.cite: Illinois High School Association, state records by sport
look.prompt: How many years separate the first boys wrestling champions from the first girls wrestling finals?

check.q: When did the IHSA crown its first boys wrestling state champions?
check.why: IHSA boys wrestling crowned its first state champions in 1937.

check.q: When did women's wrestling join the Olympic program?
check.why: Women's wrestling was first held at the 2004 Athens Games.

check.q: Why did Title IX alone not create a girls wrestling series in Illinois?
choices: It does not require a girls team in every sport
check.why: Title IX requires fair chances overall, not a team in every sport, so the IHSA had to act.

lessons.title: Girls Wrestling, 2021–22
lessons.mainIdea: The IHSA made girls wrestling its own sport in the 2021–22 season and held the first girls state finals in 2022.
reading: In the 2021–22 school year the IHSA added girls wrestling as a *sanctioned sport*, one it officially runs with a state series. Schools could now enter girls teams in girls-only meets. The first IHSA girls wrestling state finals took place in February 2022.

The IHSA did not act alone. Other state associations had added girls wrestling before Illinois, and more followed. Growing numbers of girls on boys teams showed there was interest. Each state association made its own vote and set its own rules.

The first girls state finals came in the same year as Title IX's fiftieth anniversary, June 23, 2022. The two papers on the bulletin board, the 1972 law and the new roster, came from different offices. But the second grew out of the chances the first required.

words.d: a sport a state association officially runs, with its rules and a state series
the date on which an event happened in an earlier year

look.title: Fifty Years Apart
look.text: June 23, 1972: a president signs an education law of thirty-seven words. February 2022: girls step onto the mats at the first IHSA girls wrestling state finals. Neither paper mentions the other.
look.prompt: Explain how the 1972 law and the 2022 finals are connected, even though one never names the other.

check.q: When were the first IHSA girls wrestling state finals held?
check.why: The first IHSA girls wrestling state finals were in February 2022, in the 2021–22 season.

check.q: What is a sanctioned sport?
choices: A sport played only in the Olympics
A sport a state association officially runs
check.why: A sanctioned sport is one a state association officially runs with a state series.

check.q: What anniversary fell in 2022?
check.why: Title IX was signed June 23, 1972, so 2022 was its fiftieth anniversary.

choices: Sex discrimination in federally funded education programs
All separate teams for girls and boys
review.why: Title IX bans discrimination on the basis of sex in education programs that receive federal money.
Title IX was signed in 1972; the test came in 1979, Grove City in 1984 and Cohen in 1996.

review.q: What did the Women's Division of the 1920s favor?
review.why: The Women's Division favored play days and opposed championships for girls.

choices: Restored Title IX's reach over a veto
review.why: The Civil Rights Restoration Act of 1988 passed over Reagan's veto.

review.q: How long after the first IHSA boys wrestling champions were the first girls finals held?
review.why: Boys champions date to 1937 and girls finals to 2022, 85 years apart.

review.q: How did girls' participation change right after 1972?
choices: It rose from about 294,000 to about 817,000 in one year
review.why: The NFHS counted 294,015 girls in 1971–72 and 817,073 in 1972–73.

review.q: What body ran women's college championships before the NCAA?
review.why: The AIAW, founded in 1971, ran women's college championships until 1982.

review.q: Which lawmaker was honored when Title IX was renamed in 2002?
review.why: Congress renamed it the Patsy T. Mink Equal Opportunity in Education Act.
